newsitem.title: USA: NYS comptroller sees debt service hitting $3.7 bln.
newsitem.headline: NYS comptroller sees debt service hitting $3.7 bln.

text.p: The New York State Comptroller on Tuesday faulted the fiscal 1998 budget proposed by Gov. George Pataki because annual debt service would rise to $3.7 billion though the actual sum spent on capital investments would fall.

H. Carl McCall, in prepared remarks, said the governor's plan would reverse a five-year trend toward using more pay-as-you-go spending, as Pataki's capital plan calls for the percentage of funds derived from cash to fall to 20.5 percent from 37 percent.

The fiscal monitor also criticized Pataki for proposing big tax reductions, including ones that aim to relieve the burden of high local property taxes needed to pay for schools, saying the governor had not specified how these cuts would be paid for over his four-year plan.
"More backdoor borrowing, more debt service, less concern about responsible fiscal practices...this is no way to run a government," McCall said.

Pataki's School Tax Relief Program was blasted on several other grounds, from not promising equity for different districts to giving Albany too much say over how local schools were run to failing to "re-dedicate" lottery receipts to education, an ommission that could allow such funds to be used to balance the budget, McCall warned.

The state's top auditor criticized the governor's failure to devise a strategy to help welfare recipients meet new work requirements, and his proposal to cut $300 million for higher education, a reduction McCall said was disguised by the budget's deliberately opaque presentation.

Other examples of "obfuscation" he cited included the governor's claim that General Funds spending would fall $56 million, though McCall found it actually rises by $54 million when an accounting gimmick is set aside.

McCall added the budget gap in Pataki's plan "appears to be articifically understated" while the governor failed to include a $1.3 billion surplus in fiscal 1997 in his list of one-shots for the next fiscal year.
